questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clause 5.2 (Policy); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.1 (Policies for Information Security)
questions.question: A new data protection law affecting the information security policy takes effect in March, and the policy is reviewed every November. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Ask staff to re-acknowledge the current policy text
options.B: Start an out-of-cycle review of the policy for the law
options.C: Log the new law for the scheduled November policy review
options.D: Have the CISO issue an interim memo until the November review

questions.key_concept: Policies are reviewed on a set cycle and also whenever a significant change, such as a new law, makes them outdated.
questions.pre_read: Compare the law's start date with the next scheduled review. Ask how long the policy would be out of date if management waited.
questions.correct_explanation: Policy review has two triggers: a fixed cycle and significant change. A law that takes effect in March would leave the policy out of line for about eight months if management waited for November, so a change-triggered review is needed now. Logging the law for the annual review is orderly, but it lets the organization run on an outdated policy while the law already applies.

wrong_explanations.A: Re-acknowledging the old text spreads awareness of a policy that will soon be out of line with the law. It changes nothing.
wrong_explanations.C: Holding legal changes for the scheduled review is standard upkeep. But a law taking effect in March is significant change, which triggers review off-cycle.
wrong_explanations.D: A memo gives interim guidance but is not a reviewed, approved policy; the policy itself stays out of line with the law until November.

tips: Eliminate: A only re-circulates an outdated policy, and D issues guidance that never passes the policy's review and approval.
Final two: B beats C because a significant legal change triggers review now, while the annual cycle would leave a months-long gap.
Exam cue: periodic review is a minimum; a major change in law, business or threat triggers an earlier review.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-6 (Configuration Settings); CIS Controls v8 Control 4 (Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets); COBIT 2019 BAI10 (Managed Configuration)
questions.question: An organization uses CIS Benchmarks as configuration baselines, but a legacy payroll server cannot support one required setting without breaking its application. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST approach?

options.A: Drop the setting from the standard baseline with CIO sign-off
options.B: Leave the server noncompliant until its next hardware refresh
options.C: Move the server onto an isolated network segment
options.D: Approve a documented exception with a compensating control

questions.key_concept: Configuration baselines need a formal exception process: documented, risk-accepted by the owner, and backed by compensating controls.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option keeps the deviation visible and accepted by someone accountable, rather than only reducing it technically.
questions.correct_explanation: Baselines need a managed exception path. Documenting the exception, having the risk owner accept it, and adding a compensating control keeps the deviation visible, approved and reviewed. Isolating the server may well be the right compensating control, but done alone it is an undocumented technical fix: nobody formally accepts the residual risk, and the deviation disappears from the baseline record.

wrong_explanations.A: Sign-off does not make the change sound. Dropping the setting from the standard weakens every server to accommodate one legacy system.
wrong_explanations.B: Waiting for a refresh leaves an unrecorded, unaccepted gap for an unknown period.
wrong_explanations.C: An auditor would welcome segmentation around a legacy server, but an unrecorded control tends to lapse unnoticed when the network around it changes.

tips: Eliminate: A weakens every server to suit one legacy system, and B leaves an unmanaged gap with no end date.
Final two: D beats C because a governed exception records and accepts the risk, while isolation alone is an untracked technical workaround.
Exam cue: when a system cannot meet a standard, look for a documented, approved exception with compensating controls.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.3 (Segregation of Duties)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that one accounts payable clerk can create new vendors and approve payments to them. Which recommendation BEST addresses this risk?

options.A: Rotate the clerk to another team every six months
options.B: Add a monthly management review of new-vendor payments
options.C: Assign vendor creation and payment approval to different staff
options.D: Have internal audit sample new-vendor payments each quarter

questions.key_concept: Segregation of duties prevents one person from completing a sensitive process alone; detective reviews are a fallback, not a substitute.
questions.pre_read: Name the two duties in the stem. Ask which option stops one person holding both, rather than spotting misuse later.
questions.correct_explanation: Creating a vendor and approving payments to it are incompatible duties: together they let one person set up a fictitious supplier and pay it. Separating the duties prevents that fraud path at the source. A monthly report of payments to new vendors is a useful detective control, but it finds problems only after money has left and relies on someone acting on the report.

wrong_explanations.A: Job rotation can expose fraud when a successor takes over, but until then one person still holds both incompatible duties.
wrong_explanations.B: Separation of duties prevents what review only finds. A manager's monthly check still earns its place, but no detective control replaces separation.
wrong_explanations.D: Audit sampling is periodic and detective, and it puts internal audit in the role of operating a control that management should own.

tips: Eliminate: A rotates the person but leaves both duties in one role, and D makes audit sampling stand in for management's control.
Final two: C beats B because separating the duties prevents the fraud, while a manager's monthly review only detects it afterwards.
Exam cue: when one person holds incompatible duties, prefer removing the conflict over adding a later review.

questions.framework_ref: NFPA 75 (Standard for the Fire Protection of Information Technology Equipment); NFPA 2001 (Standard on Clean Agent Fire Extinguishing Systems)
questions.question: A server room where staff regularly work needs fire suppression. Which option should the IS auditor recommend as BEST to protect people and avoid damaging the servers if it discharges?

options.A: Wet-pipe sprinklers with water held permanently in the pipes
options.B: A clean-agent gas system with very early smoke detection
options.C: Pre-action sprinklers whose dry pipes fill after two separate alarms
options.D: A carbon dioxide flooding system covering the whole room

questions.key_concept: For occupied server rooms, clean-agent gas suppression protects people and equipment; pre-action sprinklers are the preferred water-based option.
questions.pre_read: Underline the two constraints in the stem: people present and equipment damage. Test each option against both.
questions.correct_explanation: A clean-agent gas system puts out fire without water and is designed to be safe for people at its design concentration, so it protects both staff and servers, and very early smoke detection lets staff respond before discharge. Pre-action sprinklers are the safer water option because their pipes stay dry until two alarms confirm a fire, but once they discharge, water still damages the equipment.

wrong_explanations.A: Wet pipes discharge water directly onto equipment and can leak or trigger accidentally, causing the damage the stem wants to limit.
wrong_explanations.C: Pre-action reduces accidental discharge, but when it does release, water still damages the servers.
wrong_explanations.D: Carbon dioxide flooding displaces oxygen and can kill people, so it is unsuitable for a room where staff regularly work.

tips: Eliminate: A sprays water on equipment, and D endangers anyone in the room.
Final two: B beats C because a clean agent leaves equipment undamaged, while pre-action only delays water until discharge.
Exam cue: read the constraint words; people present rules out carbon dioxide, and limiting equipment damage favors a clean agent over water.

questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.2 (Physical Entry); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-2 (Physical Access Authorizations); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-3 (Physical Access Control)
questions.question: A contractor entered a restricted server room unescorted on four nights because their cleaning badge also opened that room. Which weakness should the IS auditor report as MOST significant?

options.A: Server room camera footage was reviewed once a month
options.B: The employer did not vet the contractor properly
options.C: The contractor's badge had no expiry date tied to the contract
options.D: Badge rights went beyond the contractor's cleaning role

questions.key_concept: Physical access rights must follow least privilege, so badges open only the areas each role needs.
questions.pre_read: Notice why the contractor could enter. Ask which control should have stopped that badge.
questions.correct_explanation: The contractor could enter because the badge granted access beyond what the cleaning role required, a failure of least privilege in physical access provisioning. Monthly camera review is a weakness too, but it is detective and would only have revealed the visits later; correct badge rights would have prevented them.

wrong_explanations.A: Excess access outranks slow detection. Monthly footage checks are a genuine gap, but no review speed makes up for a door that should not open.
wrong_explanations.B: Vetting reduces insider risk but does not justify server-room access for a cleaner.
wrong_explanations.C: Expiry limits how long a badge works, not which doors it opens; the contract was active on all four nights.

tips: Eliminate: B concerns the employer's vetting, and C concerns how long the badge lasts, not which doors it opens.
Final two: D beats A because correct badge rights prevent entry; camera review only detects it later.
Exam cue: physical access follows least privilege too; badges should open only what the role needs.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-14 (Environmental Controls); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PE-14(2) (Monitoring with Alarms and Notifications); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 7.11 (Supporting Utilities)
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews environmental controls for a server room hosting customer databases, where a cooling failure would cause hardware damage within minutes. Which finding is MOST significant?

options.A: Backup cooling covers two-thirds of the peak heat load
options.B: Cooling maintenance records are held by the facilities contractor
options.C: Out-of-hours temperature alarms go to a mailbox nobody monitors
options.D: Humidity readings are reviewed weekly rather than every day

questions.key_concept: Environmental alarms protect information assets only if alerts reach someone who can respond before equipment and data are damaged.
questions.pre_read: Notice damage would follow within minutes. Ask which finding means nobody would know until it was too late.
questions.correct_explanation: Environmental controls exist to protect the systems that hold information. With damage only minutes away, an out-of-hours cooling failure must reach someone who can act; an alarm sent to an unread mailbox means the first sign is failed servers and possible data loss. Partial backup cooling is a real capacity gap, but staff can shed non-critical load to stay within it, provided an alarm reaches them.

wrong_explanations.A: Backup cooling below peak load is a resilience shortfall, yet a gap that disables every response outranks one a response can offset.
wrong_explanations.B: Who holds the records is an administrative detail. The auditor can still obtain them to confirm maintenance happens.
wrong_explanations.D: Humidity matters, but weekly review of a slow-changing reading does not stop a temperature alarm reaching anyone.

tips: Eliminate: B concerns where records are kept, and D is a reasonable review interval for a slow-changing reading.
Final two: C beats A because an unseen alarm defeats every response, including the load shedding that offsets partial backup cooling.
Exam cue: a detective control protects nothing unless its alerts reach someone able to respond in time.

questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 15 (Right of Access); GDPR Article 12 (Information and Modalities for Exercise of Rights)
questions.question: A retailer receives an email from someone claiming to be a customer and asking for a copy of all personal data held about them. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Send the requester the data within one month of receiving it
options.B: Charge a standard fee before starting to process it
options.C: Verify the requester's identity before releasing any data
options.D: Refuse unless the request arrives by registered post

questions.key_concept: Data subjects have a right of access, answered within one month, but the controller must confirm identity first to avoid disclosure to impostors.
questions.pre_read: Notice the request came by email from someone claiming to be a customer. Ask what could go wrong if the retailer simply complied.
questions.correct_explanation: Releasing personal data to an impostor would itself be a breach of confidentiality, and an email claim proves nothing. GDPR lets the controller ask for information needed to confirm identity when there is reasonable doubt. Responding within one month is a real obligation, but the deadline serves the genuine customer; meeting it by sending the data to an unverified requester trades one failure for a worse one.

wrong_explanations.A: The one-month deadline is real, but sending data before confirming identity could disclose it to an impostor.
wrong_explanations.B: Access requests are normally free. A fee is allowed for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests, which nothing here suggests.
wrong_explanations.D: Demanding registered post adds a barrier the law does not require; requests can be made by reasonable means, including email.

tips: Eliminate: B charges a fee where access is normally free, and D imposes a form of request the law does not require.
Final two: C beats A because sending data to an unverified requester risks a breach, while verification still fits within the deadline.
Exam cue: before disclosing personal data on request, confirm who is asking; protecting confidentiality comes before speed.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IA-2 (Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users))
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews proposed login designs for online banking that must satisfy a multi-factor authentication requirement. Which design BEST meets it?

options.A: A password followed by a picture-based captcha puzzle to solve
options.B: A password plus a one-time code from a registered phone
options.C: A password plus answers to two personal security questions
options.D: A longer password checked against stricter complexity rules

questions.key_concept: Multi-factor authentication combines factors from different categories (knowledge, possession, inherence); several knowledge checks are still single-factor.
questions.pre_read: Label each element as something you know, have or are. Then count categories, not steps.
questions.correct_explanation: Multi-factor authentication needs factors from different categories: something you know, something you have and something you are. A password plus a code from an app on a registered phone combines knowledge with possession. Security questions add more checks, but they are just more things the user knows, so a password plus questions is still single-factor and falls to the same phishing or data leak.

wrong_explanations.A: A captcha checks that a human is present, not which human. It adds no authentication factor.
wrong_explanations.C: Security questions are another knowledge factor. Two things you know remain one factor category, so this is not multi-factor.
wrong_explanations.D: A stronger password is still one knowledge factor. Complexity improves it but does not add a second category.

tips: Eliminate: A adds a bot check, not an identity factor, and D only strengthens the single password.
Final two: B beats C because a registered phone adds a possession factor, while security questions are just more knowledge.
Exam cue: count factor categories, not checks; multi-factor needs two of know, have and are.

questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clause 4.3 (Determining the Scope of the Information Security Management System); PCI DSS v4.0.1
questions.question: An IS auditor finds a company's ISO/IEC 27001 certificate scope excludes the call center, where staff take card payments by phone. Which concern is MOST significant?

options.A: The certificate gives no assurance over the call center's card handling
options.B: The certification body should not have issued this certificate to the company
options.C: Call center staff have not completed security awareness training
options.D: Card payment rules no longer apply to the call center

questions.key_concept: A certificate covers only its defined scope; relying parties must check that high-risk areas are inside it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a certificate does and does not tell people who rely on it.
questions.correct_explanation: An ISO/IEC 27001 certificate covers only the scope the organization defined, so it says nothing about how the call center protects card data. Customers, partners and management may rely on the certificate as if it covered that high-risk area. Challenging the certificate itself is the closest choice, but organizations may set their scope; the issue is the assurance gap and whether the exclusion is justified.

wrong_explanations.B: Organizations may define their own ISMS scope, and certification covers what was assessed. The exclusion creates an assurance gap, not an invalid certificate.
wrong_explanations.C: Training is a separate control. Even fully trained staff would not bring the call center inside the certificate's scope, so the assurance gap would remain.
wrong_explanations.D: Card payment obligations apply wherever card data is handled, whatever the ISMS scope says.

tips: Eliminate: C swaps a scope question for a training question, and D wrongly assumes scope removes industry obligations.
Final two: A beats B because a narrow scope is allowed; the risk is that people rely on assurance it does not provide.
Exam cue: always check what a certificate or assurance report covers before relying on it.

questions.subtopic: Lost Device Remote Wipe. Evidence of Execution
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-124 Rev 2 (Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-19 (Access Control for Mobile Devices)
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews 25 lost-phone cases where the device management console shows a remote wipe as sent. Which finding should concern the auditor MOST?

options.A: Nine wipes were never confirmed as completed on the device
options.B: Lost devices were reported up to four hours after loss
options.C: Wipe commands were sent by the help desk, not security
options.D: Users were not asked to sign a lost-device form

questions.key_concept: A wipe command protects data only once the device carries it out; the auditor looks for evidence of completion.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether sending a command proves the data was removed.
questions.correct_explanation: A wipe command only protects data once the device receives and carries it out; a phone kept offline never does. Nine unconfirmed wipes mean there is no evidence the control worked, and nobody followed up on devices that may still hold company data. Reporting delays of a few hours are the closest concern: they widen the exposure window, but a wipe that never runs leaves the exposure open indefinitely.

wrong_explanations.B: Delays widen the window before the wipe is sent, but a confirmed wipe still closes it; an unconfirmed one may never close it.
wrong_explanations.C: Who sends the command matters less than whether it worked; help desk execution under a defined process is common and acceptable.
wrong_explanations.D: A missing form is a paperwork gap and does nothing to show whether the data on the lost phone was removed.

tips: Eliminate: C questions who sent the command rather than whether it worked, and D is a paperwork gap that does not affect whether data was wiped.
Final two: A beats B because a delay narrows protection, while an unconfirmed wipe may mean the data was never protected.
Exam cue: a control that was triggered is not a control that worked; look for evidence of completion.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.2 (Privileged Access Rights); CIS Controls v8 Control 6 (Access Control Management)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds domain administrators hold permanent standing rights, protected by hardware-token multi-factor authentication. Which recommendation BEST reduces the remaining risk?

options.A: Vault administrator passwords and rotate them automatically after each use
options.B: Review weekly logs of how administrators use their rights
options.C: Lengthen administrator passwords to at least twenty characters
options.D: Grant administrator rights on approval, for a limited period

questions.key_concept: Just-in-time elevation removes standing privilege: rights are granted on approval for a limited time, applying least privilege to time as well as scope.
questions.pre_read: Notice that authentication is already strong. Ask what risk remains when the rights never go away.
questions.correct_explanation: Strong authentication already protects the login, so the remaining exposure is that powerful rights exist all the time, even when no administrative work is under way. Just-in-time elevation applies least privilege to time: rights appear only after approval and expire automatically. Vaulting and rotating passwords protects the credential itself, but the accounts still hold permanent rights for anyone who hijacks a session.

wrong_explanations.A: Vaulting protects the credential, but the accounts keep permanent domain rights that a hijacked session or an insider can use at any time.
wrong_explanations.B: Weekly log review detects misuse after it happens, and the permanent rights stay available to an attacker or insider between reviews.
wrong_explanations.C: Hardware-token authentication already protects the login. Longer passwords add little and leave the rights permanently available.

tips: Eliminate: B reviews misuse after the fact while rights stay permanent, and C adds little on top of hardware-token authentication.
Final two: D beats A because removing standing privilege limits misuse at all times, while vaulting only protects the password.
Exam cue: when authentication is already strong, look at how long privilege lasts; least privilege applies to time as well as scope.

questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A.5.12 (Classification of information); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.12 (Classification of Information)
questions.question: After a merger, an IS auditor finds each business unit labels information with its own classification levels, so shared data gets inconsistent protection. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Keep each unit's scheme and publish an approved mapping between them
options.B: Apply the strictest unit's highest label to shared data
options.C: Adopt one company-wide classification scheme with handling rules
options.D: Have IT decide protection levels for shared data stores

questions.key_concept: One approved organization-wide classification scheme, with handling rules per level, gives every unit the same labels and protection.
questions.pre_read: Ask what makes a label mean the same thing in every part of the company.
questions.correct_explanation: A single organization-wide classification scheme, approved by management and paired with handling rules for each level, gives every unit the same meaning for each label and the same protection for shared data. Keeping separate schemes with a published mapping is the most tempting alternative; it can help during transition, but people must translate labels at every handoff, and mismatched levels keep producing gaps.

wrong_explanations.A: A mapping, like one scheme, gives labels agreed meaning, but it manages the inconsistency rather than removing it. Fix a variance at its source.
wrong_explanations.B: Labeling everything at the top level over-protects routine data, raises cost and teaches staff to ignore labels.
wrong_explanations.D: IT can implement protection, but data owners decide sensitivity; a technical team choosing levels skips business ownership.

tips: Eliminate: B over-classifies everything, and D gives IT a decision that belongs to data owners.
Final two: C beats A because one scheme gives each label the same meaning everywhere, while a mapping keeps the translation gaps.
Exam cue: classification starts with one approved scheme and handling rules; owners then apply it to their data.

questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev 1 (Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy); NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-7 (Boundary Protection); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.22 (Segregation of Networks)
questions.question: An IS auditor finds a public-facing web server sits on the same internal network segment as the customer database. Which recommendation BEST reduces the risk?

options.A: Add host-based intrusion detection to the web server
options.B: Place the web server in a filtered screened subnet
options.C: Harden the web server's configuration to a secure baseline
options.D: Require multi-factor login for the web server's administrators

questions.key_concept: Internet-facing systems belong in a screened subnet, with only filtered connections to internal zones holding sensitive data.
questions.pre_read: Notice which system faces the internet and what sits beside it. Ask what an attacker could reach after compromising it.
questions.correct_explanation: A public web server is the system most exposed to attack, so the design must assume it may be breached. Placing it in a screened subnet, often called a DMZ, with only specific filtered connections to the database zone limits what an attacker can reach from it. Hardening the server lowers the chance of compromise, but if it is still breached, nothing stands between the attacker and customer data.

wrong_explanations.A: Intrusion detection may spot an attack, but a breached server on the flat segment still has a direct path to the database.
wrong_explanations.C: Hardening lowers the likelihood of compromise, but a breached server on a flat segment still has an open path to the customer database.
wrong_explanations.D: Stronger admin login protects one route in, but the web application itself is the exposed target, and the flat segment remains.

tips: Eliminate: A detects an attack without limiting where it can go, and D protects administrator logins rather than the exposed application.
Final two: B beats C because zoning limits what a breached server can reach; hardening only lowers the odds of the breach itself.
Exam cue: assume exposed systems will be breached; separate them from sensitive data instead of relying only on making them harder to break into.

questions.question: A data owner is concerned that staff copy confidential client files to USB drives on laptops used away from the corporate network. Which control should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Endpoint data loss prevention enforcing policy on each device
options.B: Network data loss prevention inspecting traffic at the internet gateway
options.C: A web application firewall placed in front of the client portal
options.D: Quarterly owner reviews of file shares to locate confidential client files

questions.key_concept: Endpoint data loss prevention controls removable media and local actions on the device itself, including when it is off the corporate network.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the copying happens and where the laptops are. Ask which control can see that channel.
questions.correct_explanation: The copying happens on the laptop itself, often while it is off the corporate network. Endpoint data loss prevention runs on the device, so it can see and block transfers to USB drives wherever the laptop is. Network data loss prevention is a real control for email and web uploads, but it only inspects traffic that passes the gateway and never sees a local copy to removable media.

wrong_explanations.B: Gateway inspection covers traffic leaving through the network. A file copied to a USB drive, especially off-network, never passes the gateway.
wrong_explanations.C: A web application firewall protects the portal against web attacks. It has no view of files staff copy on their laptops.
wrong_explanations.D: Owner reviews find where confidential data is stored. They do not block it being copied to removable media.

tips: Eliminate: C protects a web application from attacks, and D locates stored data without stopping any copying.
Final two: A beats B because the copying happens on the device, often off-network, where gateway inspection never sees it.
Exam cue: match the data loss prevention type to the leak channel; endpoint for local devices, network for traffic, discovery for stored data.

questions.question: After microsegmentation went live, developers began adding allow-any rules without approval to fix outages. Which recommendation should the IS auditor make to BEST address this?

options.A: Let developers add rules and review the changes each month
options.B: Put segmentation rule changes under formal change management
options.C: Retrain developers on the purpose of the segmentation policy
options.D: Alert the security team whenever an allow-any rule is added

questions.key_concept: Segmentation rules need change control; unapproved allow-any rules quietly undo microsegmentation's protection against lateral movement.
questions.pre_read: Notice the problem is how rules are changed, not the design. Ask which option stops bad rules before they go in.
questions.correct_explanation: The design is sound; the weakness is that anyone can loosen it under pressure without review. Routing rule changes through change management, with security approval and an emergency path, stops allow-any rules going in while still letting teams fix genuine outages. Retraining raises awareness, but during an outage developers will still take the quickest fix if nothing requires approval.

wrong_explanations.A: Monthly review finds bad rules weeks later; an allow-any rule opens lateral movement from the moment it is added.
wrong_explanations.C: Awareness helps, but under outage pressure people take the fastest route. Without an approval gate, nothing stops the next allow-any rule.
wrong_explanations.D: An alert fires once the rule is live. Nothing stops it going in, and security must chase each one afterward.

tips: Eliminate: A and D both find bad rules after they are live, which detects the change rather than preventing it.
Final two: B beats C because an approval gate holds under pressure, while training relies on developers choosing to comply.
Exam cue: when a sound control is weakened by unapproved changes, enforce the change process; awareness alone will not hold under pressure.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that, under a new zero trust program, users who pass the VPN login still reach every internal application without further checks. Which recommendation BEST aligns with NIST SP 800-207?

options.A: Add a second VPN concentrator to improve remote access resilience
options.B: Protect the VPN login with phishing-resistant authentication
options.C: Block remote access to internal applications outside office hours
options.D: Authorize each application request using identity and device health

questions.key_concept: Zero trust evaluates every access request using identity, device and context, rather than trusting users once they are on the network.
questions.pre_read: Notice what happens after users pass the VPN. Ask which option removes that remaining implicit trust.
questions.correct_explanation: Zero trust removes implicit trust based on network location. Under NIST SP 800-207, each access request is evaluated by a policy decision point using identity, device state and context, and enforced per resource. Here the VPN still grants broad trust once someone is inside. Stronger VPN authentication makes that one gate harder to pass, but everyone who passes still reaches everything.

wrong_explanations.A: A second concentrator improves the availability of remote access. It leaves the implicit trust given to connected users unchanged.
wrong_explanations.B: Stronger login protection helps, but anyone who passes it, including a hijacked session, still reaches every application without further checks.
wrong_explanations.C: Time-of-day limits reduce exposure slightly but still trust anyone connected during office hours.

tips: Eliminate: A improves availability rather than trust decisions, and C only narrows when implicit trust applies.
Final two: D beats B because zero trust evaluates every request, while a stronger VPN login still trusts everyone once inside.
Exam cue: zero trust moves decisions from the network edge to each resource request; a better perimeter is still a perimeter.

questions.question: Every company laptop uses full-disk encryption, and field staff regularly copy client files onto USB drives for site visits. Which control gap should the IS auditor recommend addressing FIRST?

options.A: Laptop disk encryption keys are not changed every year
options.B: Encrypted laptops unlock with the hardware chip alone, without a PIN
options.C: Desktop computers inside locked offices are not encrypted
options.D: USB drives carrying client files leave the office unencrypted

questions.key_concept: Encryption must follow sensitive data onto every portable medium; full-disk encryption on laptops does not protect copies on removable drives.
questions.pre_read: Notice where client files travel after they leave the laptop. Ask which copy has no protection at all if lost.
questions.correct_explanation: Client files copied to USB drives leave the protection of laptop disk encryption entirely, and small drives are easily lost on site visits, so a lost drive exposes the data in clear. Unlocking laptops with the hardware chip alone weakens protection against a skilled attacker, but the disk is still encrypted. An unprotected copy of sensitive data outranks a hardening improvement to protected devices.

wrong_explanations.A: Annual rotation of disk encryption keys is not a standard requirement. The laptops remain encrypted and protected.
wrong_explanations.B: Adding a pre-boot PIN strengthens laptop protection, but the disk is already encrypted, while the USB copies have no protection.
wrong_explanations.C: Desktops in locked offices face lower theft risk than portable media, and physical controls already protect them.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a rotation rule that does not apply, and C covers devices already shielded by locked offices.
Final two: D beats B because the USB copies have no encryption at all, while chip-only unlock still leaves disks encrypted.
Exam cue: follow the sensitive data. The copy that leaves an encrypted device unprotected is usually the biggest gap.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds an application encrypts customer records using AES in ECB mode with a 128-bit key. Which recommendation BEST addresses the weakness?

options.A: Rotate the AES encryption key every thirty days
options.B: Switch to AES in GCM mode, which also verifies integrity
options.C: Switch to AES in CBC mode with one fixed initialization vector
options.D: Increase the AES key length from 128 bits to 256 bits

questions.key_concept: ECB mode leaks patterns because identical blocks encrypt identically; an authenticated mode such as GCM fixes this and adds integrity.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem names both a mode and a key length. Ask which of the two is actually weak.
questions.correct_explanation: ECB encrypts identical plaintext blocks to identical ciphertext, so structured records leak patterns whatever the key length. GCM uses a unique nonce per message to hide patterns and adds an authentication tag that detects tampering. A 256-bit key sounds stronger, but a 128-bit AES key is already secure; the weakness is the mode, which a longer key does not change.

wrong_explanations.A: Rotating the key does not stop ECB repeating patterns within the data encrypted under each key.
wrong_explanations.C: A fixed initialization vector makes identical records encrypt identically again, and CBC alone gives no integrity.
wrong_explanations.D: AES-128 is not the weakness. ECB leaks patterns at any key length, so a longer key leaves the flaw in place.

tips: Eliminate: A rotates keys without fixing the mode, and C reintroduces repetition with a fixed initialization vector.
Final two: B beats D because ECB leaks patterns at any key length; the mode, not the key size, is weak.
Exam cue: when ECB appears, the fix is the mode; prefer an authenticated mode such as GCM.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds a payment portal accepts TLS 1.0, 1.2 and 1.3, and many customers still use browsers that support TLS 1.2 but not 1.3. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Keep accepting every version so older browsers keep working
options.B: Replace TLS 1.0 with TLS 1.1 for customers on older browsers
options.C: Disable TLS 1.0 and restrict TLS 1.2 to strong cipher suites
options.D: Disable TLS 1.0 and 1.2, leaving TLS 1.3 as the sole version

questions.key_concept: Remove deprecated protocol versions, and keep TLS 1.2 only with strong cipher suites when customers still need it alongside TLS 1.3.
questions.pre_read: Notice what many customers' browsers support. Ask which change removes the weakness without blocking legitimate users.
questions.correct_explanation: TLS 1.0 is deprecated and must go. Under PCI DSS (the card industry's security standard), TLS 1.2 remains acceptable with strong cipher suites (the algorithm sets a connection uses), so keeping it alongside 1.3 removes the real weakness while customers can still pay. Accepting only TLS 1.3 is strictest, but it would lock out many legitimate customers without fixing any weakness in properly configured TLS 1.2.

wrong_explanations.A: TLS 1.0 is deprecated and exposed to known attacks. Keeping it fails PCI DSS and leaves card data at risk.
wrong_explanations.B: TLS 1.1 is deprecated as well. Swapping one retired version for another keeps the same class of weakness and still fails PCI DSS.
wrong_explanations.D: TLS 1.3 alone would win once customers' browsers catch up. Until then, the stricter setting buys little, and controls should not exceed the risk.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps a deprecated protocol, and B swaps it for TLS 1.1, which is also deprecated.
Final two: C beats D because a strong TLS 1.2 setup is still acceptable, and cutting it blocks the many customers who rely on it.
Exam cue: remove a protocol the governing standard already prohibits, harden what remains acceptable, and weigh the stated business fact.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews code signing for software released to customers. Which finding should concern the auditor MOST?

options.A: The signing certificate expires in eleven months and has a renewal plan
options.B: Release notes published with each version are not digitally signed
options.C: The private signing key sits on a build server all developers access
options.D: Released files are signed without a trusted time-stamp authority

questions.key_concept: A signature is only as trustworthy as custody of the signing key; a widely accessible key lets anyone sign malicious code.
questions.pre_read: Notice who could use the signing key. Ask what customers trust when they see a valid signature.
questions.correct_explanation: Customers trust any code carrying the firm's signature, so whoever can use the private key can ship trusted malware. A key on a build server every developer can reach has no meaningful custody and should be in a hardware module with controlled use. Missing time-stamps cause valid signatures to fail after the certificate expires, an availability problem rather than a trust breach.

wrong_explanations.A: A certificate with eleven months left and a renewal plan is being managed properly.
wrong_explanations.B: Release notes are not executable code. Leaving them unsigned is a minor gap compared with code signing itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Without time-stamps, signatures fail after certificate expiry, a disruption, but forged code is not made trustworthy.

tips: Eliminate: A shows a managed renewal, and B concerns documents that customers do not execute.
Final two: C beats D because exposed key custody lets anyone sign malware, while missing time-stamps cause later failures.
Exam cue: in any signature review, check who can use the private key before anything else.

options.A: Internal websites whose certificates are due to expire soonest
options.B: Links carrying data that must stay confidential for decades
options.C: Storage already encrypted with AES using 256-bit keys
options.D: Systems handling the highest daily transaction volumes

questions.key_concept: Harvest-now-decrypt-later means long-lived confidential data sent with today's public-key cryptography is the first post-quantum priority.
questions.pre_read: Notice the threat is future decryption of data captured today. Ask which data would still matter when that becomes possible.
questions.correct_explanation: Attackers can record encrypted traffic now and decrypt it once quantum computers break today's public-key key exchange. Data that must stay confidential for decades is exposed to that harvest-now-decrypt-later threat already, so its links move first. High-volume systems feel critical, but volume does not measure how long the data must stay secret, which is what this threat exploits.

wrong_explanations.A: Certificate expiry dates set renewal schedules, not quantum risk. Short-lived internal data is a low priority.
wrong_explanations.C: AES with 256-bit keys is expected to remain secure against quantum attacks, so it needs little change.
wrong_explanations.D: Ranking by volume works for availability planning. Priorities set for one threat, though, do not carry over to another.

tips: Eliminate: A ranks by expiry dates, and C targets symmetric encryption that already resists quantum attack.
Final two: B beats D because the quantum threat targets long-lived secrets, whatever the transaction volume.
Exam cue: for post-quantum priorities, ask how long the data must stay secret, not how busy the system is.

questions.question: A merchant's payment team wants to remove stored card numbers from most systems to reduce PCI DSS scope, while refunds still need the original card. Which method should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Replace card numbers with tokens mapped in a secure vault
options.B: Store an unsalted hash of each card number instead
options.C: Truncate stored card numbers to their last four digits
options.D: Encrypt card numbers in every system with centrally managed keys

questions.key_concept: Tokenization removes card numbers from most systems, shrinking PCI DSS scope, while the vault still allows authorized recovery.
questions.pre_read: Notice two needs: fewer systems holding card numbers, and the ability to refund. Ask which method meets both.
questions.correct_explanation: Tokenization replaces card numbers with tokens that are useless outside the vault, so systems holding only tokens can fall out of PCI DSS scope, while the vault returns the real number for refunds. Encryption with managed keys protects card numbers well, but every system holding encrypted card data and its key access generally stays in scope, so it misses the stated goal.

wrong_explanations.B: Card numbers have limited variety, so unsalted hashes are easily brute-forced, and a hash cannot be reversed for refunds.
wrong_explanations.C: Truncated numbers cannot process refunds against the original card, which the stem requires.
wrong_explanations.D: Centrally keyed encryption is a prudent safeguard for stored card numbers, yet protection is not removal; scope shrinks where card data leaves a system.

tips: Eliminate: B is crackable and irreversible, and C cannot support the refunds the stem requires.
Final two: A beats D because tokens take systems out of scope, while encrypted card data keeps them in it.
Exam cue: when the goal is scope reduction with later retrieval, think tokenization rather than encryption or hashing.

options.B: Change every recovery key automatically at the end of each calendar month

Limiting access to two senior agents reduces insider misuse, but those agents can still be talked into releasing a key to an impostor, because nobody checks who is calling.

wrong_explanations.B: Monthly key changes add workload but do not stop a key being handed to an unverified caller.
wrong_explanations.C: Fewer agents reduce insider misuse, but without caller verification they can still release keys to an impostor.

tips: Eliminate: A records releases for later review rather than stopping them, and B changes keys without fixing who receives them.

questions.question: Ransomware is deleting a hospital's backup keys from its networked vault at 2% per minute; a week-old offline backup has its own keys. Which action would the IS auditor expect management to take FIRST?

options.A: Isolate the backup key vault from the network immediately
options.B: Start restoring systems from the week-old offline backup
options.C: Rotate the vault's administrator credentials while it stays online
options.D: Scan production storage to identify the ransomware variant

questions.key_concept: Contain an active incident before recovery: stopping ongoing damage preserves more recoverable data than restoring from an older backup.
questions.pre_read: Note the damage is still happening. Ask which action stops it, and which ones only analyze or recover.
questions.correct_explanation: Containment comes first. Cutting the key vault off the network stops the erasure while most keys survive, which keeps recent backups recoverable and avoids losing a week of hospital data. Restoring from the offline copy is recovery, and starting it while the ransomware is still active risks reinfecting restored systems and needlessly accepts seven days of data loss.

wrong_explanations.B: An isolated offline backup is the backbone of ransomware recovery. While keys are still vanishing, isolating the vault saves more: recovery follows containment.
wrong_explanations.C: New credentials may close one access path, but ransomware already running keeps deleting keys while the vault stays connected.
wrong_explanations.D: Identifying the variant supports later eradication, but analysis while keys disappear at 2% per minute lets the damage continue.

tips: Eliminate: C changes credentials while the vault stays reachable, and D analyzes the malware while keys keep disappearing.
Final two: A beats B because containment stops the loss now, while restoring first is recovery before the threat is contained.
Exam cue: in incidents, contain before eradicating and before recovering, especially when damage is still spreading.

options.B: Users can open other users' invoices by changing a number

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the security of a private cloud running about 900 virtual machines. Which finding should concern the auditor MOST?

options.A: Virtual machine templates are reviewed annually rather than quarterly
options.B: Virtual machine snapshots are retained on the production storage arrays
options.C: Hosts run workloads from different business units side by side
options.D: The hypervisor management console is reachable from the office network

questions.key_concept: The hypervisor management plane controls every virtual machine, so it must sit on a restricted, isolated management network.
questions.pre_read: Ask which single weakness would let one person control all 900 virtual machines at once.
questions.correct_explanation: Whoever reaches the management console can start, copy or reconfigure every virtual machine, so exposing it to the general office network puts the whole platform at risk. Sharing hosts between business units is normal in virtualization; the hypervisor is designed to isolate guests, and that isolation is maintained through patching and hardening.

wrong_explanations.A: Annual template review is a modest cadence choice. Templates are still reviewed, and the gap does not expose any running system.
wrong_explanations.B: Keeping snapshots on production storage is mainly an availability and recovery concern, not a direct path to compromising the platform.
wrong_explanations.C: Running units on shared hosts is normal virtualization design; hypervisor isolation separates the guests, so this alone is not a control failure.

tips: Eliminate: A is a review-frequency choice for templates that are still reviewed, and B is a recovery-design point rather than a security exposure.
Final two: D beats C because the management console controls every virtual machine, while shared hosting is normal and relies on hypervisor isolation.
Exam cue: in virtualization, protect the management plane first; whoever controls it controls every guest.

questions.question: An IS auditor notes that a banking website redirects visitors from HTTP to HTTPS, leaving each first request open to interception. Which control BEST closes this gap?

options.A: A content security policy limiting where scripts may load from
options.B: A secure flag on every session cookie the site issues
options.C: A strict transport security header with the domain preloaded
options.D: A frame options header stopping the site loading inside other pages

questions.key_concept: HTTP Strict Transport Security, with preloading, makes browsers use HTTPS from the first request and defeats protocol-stripping attacks.
questions.pre_read: Focus on the first request. Ask which header stops the browser from sending it over plain HTTP at all.
questions.correct_explanation: HTTP Strict Transport Security tells browsers to use HTTPS for the domain without trying HTTP first, and preloading protects even the very first visit, so attackers cannot strip the redirect. A secure cookie flag keeps session cookies off plain HTTP, which is valuable, but the unencrypted first request can still be intercepted and redirected to a fake page.

wrong_explanations.A: A content security policy limits script sources to reduce cross-site scripting; it does not force browsers onto HTTPS.
wrong_explanations.B: The secure flag is an established cookie safeguard, yet protecting one item on a channel is not the same as securing the channel.
wrong_explanations.D: Frame options prevent clickjacking by blocking framing; they do nothing about the unencrypted first request.

tips: Eliminate: A addresses cross-site scripting, and D addresses clickjacking; neither touches the unencrypted first request.
Final two: C beats B because the transport header removes the plain HTTP request itself, while the cookie flag protects only the cookie.
Exam cue: match each header to its threat; for downgrade or stripping attacks, the answer is strict transport security.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a wireless intrusion detection system covering 14 offices. Which finding should concern the auditor MOST?

options.A: Sensor firmware reviews and updates happen quarterly, not monthly
options.B: Rogue access point alerts are logged but nobody reviews them
options.C: Sensors cover about 85 percent of each office's floor area
options.D: The corporate network names are broadcast rather than hidden

questions.key_concept: A detective control only works if its alerts are reviewed and acted upon; unreviewed alerts give false assurance.
questions.pre_read: Ask which finding makes the system useless in every office, rather than weaker in some places.
questions.correct_explanation: Detection has value only when someone responds. Rogue access point alerts that nobody reviews mean an attacker's device could sit on the network indefinitely in all 14 offices, so the control effectively provides no protection. Partial sensor coverage leaves blind spots, but alerts from the covered 85 percent would still lead to action if anyone were reviewing them.

wrong_explanations.A: Slower firmware updates can look risky, but the sensors still detect rogue devices; unreviewed alerts mean detected rogue access points are never acted on.
wrong_explanations.C: Coverage gaps create blind spots, but most of each office is still monitored; unreviewed alerts mean nothing is acted on anywhere.
wrong_explanations.D: Hiding network names is obscurity that offers little protection, so broadcasting them is not a significant weakness.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because A is a routine update interval for sensors that still work, and D treats hiding network names as security when it is only obscurity.
Final two: B beats C because unreviewed alerts disable the control everywhere, while partial coverage weakens it in some areas.
Exam cue: a detective control without follow-up is effectively absent; check that alerts are reviewed and acted on.

questions.question: Reviewing a past incident, an IS auditor finds staff powered down botnet-infected building-control devices, so 14 stores opened without heating or door controls. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Have stores reboot infected devices to clear the infection
options.B: Update the playbook to block such devices' internet traffic
options.C: Add the building devices to the monthly vulnerability scan
options.D: Keep spare devices at each store for quick replacement

questions.key_concept: Proportionate containment cuts the harmful traffic path while essential operations keep running, rather than shutting every affected device down.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the shutdown cost the stores. Ask which response would stop the attack without that cost.
questions.correct_explanation: Blocking the devices' internet traffic stops the attack traffic while heating and door controls keep working locally, so the stores could have opened normally. The response playbook should make that proportionate step the default for compromised building devices. Keeping spares shortens an outage after a shutdown, but it accepts the outage and the swap work; blocking traffic avoids the outage altogether.

wrong_explanations.A: Botnet malware often persists in firmware or returns at once through the same flaw, so a reboot neither contains nor removes it.
wrong_explanations.C: Scanning finds weaknesses for later patching; it does not tell staff how to contain a device that is attacking right now.
wrong_explanations.D: Spares and traffic blocking both aim to keep stores open. When the response caused the outage, change the response rather than stock for it.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a reboot removes persistent malware, and C adds detection without changing how staff contain an attack.
Final two: B beats D because spares only shorten the outage, while a playbook that blocks internet traffic stops the attack with no outage.
Exam cue: judge containment by whether it stopped the harm with the least disruption; cut the harmful path, not the whole service.

options.A: Posters in common areas are refreshed twice a year
options.B: Training is delivered online rather than in classrooms
options.C: Completion is tracked by attendance rather than by quiz results
options.D: Privileged administrators receive only the general staff course

questions.key_concept: Security awareness must be role-based, with deeper training for privileged and high-risk roles than for general staff.
questions.pre_read: Ask which group could do the most damage, and whether the program prepares that group for its risks.
questions.correct_explanation: Awareness training should be tailored to risk. Privileged administrators can cause the greatest damage through error or social engineering, so giving them only the general course leaves the highest-risk group without the role-specific knowledge they need. Measuring attendance rather than quiz results weakens evidence of learning, but staff are still trained; it is a measurement gap, not a coverage gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Poster refresh frequency is a minor delivery detail; posters supplement training rather than replace it.
wrong_explanations.B: Online delivery is a common, effective format; the delivery channel alone is not a control weakness.
wrong_explanations.C: Quiz scores are an accepted learning measure. Better proof, though, leaves a control unchanged: fix what a control does before how it is evidenced.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are delivery details that do not weaken what staff learn.
Final two: D beats C because the highest-risk group lacks role-specific training, while attendance tracking only weakens measurement.
Exam cue: awareness programs should be role-based; gaps affecting privileged users outrank gaps in how completion is measured.

options.B: Stop penalizing clicks and recognize staff who report phishing
options.C: Add remedial training for staff who click on simulations repeatedly
options.D: Publish department click rankings to encourage friendly competition

questions.key_concept: Phishing simulations should build a reporting culture; punishing clicks suppresses the reports that catch real attacks early.
questions.pre_read: Notice which number got worse. Ask which change restores reporting, rather than improving the click rate.
questions.correct_explanation: Reporting is how real attacks get caught early, and fear of punishment has halved it. Removing penalties and recognizing reporters rebuilds the culture in which staff speak up. Remedial training for repeat clickers is a supportive measure worth keeping, but while discipline remains, staff will still hide mistakes and avoid reporting.

wrong_explanations.A: Harder simulations may raise clicks again but do nothing about the fear that is suppressing reports of real phishing.
wrong_explanations.C: Remedial training helps repeat clickers, but it leaves the punitive policy in place, so staff still avoid reporting.
wrong_explanations.D: Public rankings still shame clickers, so staff keep hiding mistakes; the fear that suppresses reporting stays in place.

tips: Eliminate: A changes the test difficulty without fixing the culture, and D keeps public shaming, which still suppresses reporting.
Final two: B beats C because removing the penalty restores reporting, while remedial training leaves the fear in place.
Exam cue: in awareness programs, the reporting rate matters more than the click rate; avoid measures that discourage reporting.

questions.question: A treasury analyst flags a $2.4M wire, emailed by the traveling CEO, to an overseas account opened 14 days ago. With settlement in 45 minutes, what should the IS auditor recommend management do FIRST?

options.A: Hold the wire until the CEO confirms on a known phone number
options.B: Reply to the CEO's email asking to confirm the payment
options.C: Release the wire once a second treasury officer approves it
options.D: Call finance, legal and security leaders together to agree a response

questions.key_concept: In suspected business email compromise, stop the irreversible payment first and verify through a separate, known channel.
questions.pre_read: Notice the 45-minute settlement window and the new overseas account. Ask which action stops an irreversible loss.
questions.correct_explanation: The red flags point to business email compromise, and a settled wire is rarely recovered. Treasury should hold the payment and verify with the CEO on a phone number already on file, a channel the attacker does not control. Convening leaders is sensible later, but while they meet the settlement deadline passes, so stopping the loss comes first.

wrong_explanations.B: If the CEO's email is compromised or spoofed, replying goes to the attacker, who will simply confirm the payment.
wrong_explanations.C: Dual approval is a familiar payment control, but both officers see the same spoofed email; neither confirms the CEO sent it, and released funds are rarely recovered.
wrong_explanations.D: Coordination matters later, but while the meeting runs, the queued wire can settle within the 45-minute window.

tips: Eliminate: B and C, because B verifies through the channel the attacker may control, and C adds a second approver who never confirms the CEO sent it.
Final two: A beats D because the settlement deadline makes stopping the payment the priority; a meeting would let the wire leave.
Exam cue: when a loss is irreversible and time-bound, the FIRST action stops it, then verify through a known channel.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds developers can mark static analysis findings as false positives with no one else reviewing them. Which control BEST addresses this?

options.A: Run the static analysis tool on every commit instead of nightly
options.B: Have another developer on the team approve each suppression
options.C: Train developers to recognize genuine false positives
options.D: Require security team approval for each suppressed finding

questions.key_concept: Suppressing a security finding is an exception that needs independent approval; the person whose code is flagged should not close it alone.
questions.pre_read: Notice who suppresses the findings and who checks them. Ask which control restores independence.
questions.correct_explanation: Developers dismissing findings in their own code with no review is a segregation of duties gap: real vulnerabilities can be suppressed unnoticed. Requiring security team approval for each suppression adds an independent, expert check. Approval by another developer adds a second person, but a teammate shares the same delivery pressure and usually lacks security expertise, so the review is not truly independent.

wrong_explanations.A: Scanning more often produces findings sooner, but developers could still dismiss them with no review.
wrong_explanations.B: Peer approval is a mainstay of code review, but independence means no stake in the outcome, and a fellow developer ships the same release.
wrong_explanations.C: Better judgment helps, but developers would still decide alone on their own code's findings, leaving the independence gap open.

tips: Eliminate: A changes scan timing while suppressions stay unreviewed, and C improves judgment but leaves the developer deciding alone.
Final two: D beats B because the security team is independent of the code's delivery; a teammate shares the same pressure and blind spots.
Exam cue: when people can approve exceptions to their own work, the fix is an independent approver, not just a second pair of hands.

questions.question: An IS auditor must assess whether SIEM detection rules written two years ago still detect attacks in today's environment. Which test provides the BEST evidence?

options.A: Confirm the SIEM vendor still supports the current software version
options.B: Run simulated attacks and confirm each expected alert is raised
options.C: Read each rule's logic against the original design documents
options.D: Count the alerts each rule generated over the past year

questions.key_concept: Detection rules decay as environments change; simulated attacks show whether they still fire, stronger evidence than reviewing their design.
questions.pre_read: Notice the rules are two years old. Ask which test shows they work today, not only how they were written.
questions.correct_explanation: Rules can silently break as log sources, field names and systems change. Running simulated attack techniques in the live environment and checking that each expected alert appears tests operating effectiveness directly. Reading the rule logic against design documents shows how each rule was meant to work, but a rule that looks correct on paper can still miss attacks if its log source has changed or stopped.

wrong_explanations.A: Vendor support matters for maintenance, but a supported product can still run rules that no longer match today's logs.
wrong_explanations.C: A logic review is how an auditor tests rule design. Whether rules still fire is operating effectiveness, which only a live test shows.
wrong_explanations.D: Alert counts show activity, not accuracy. A noisy rule can fire often while missing the attack it was built for.

tips: Eliminate: A checks vendor support rather than detection, and D counts alerts rather than testing them.
Final two: B beats C because a simulation proves the rule fires today, while a logic review shows only the intended design.
Exam cue: to show a control works now, prefer evidence that tests it in operation over a review of its design.

questions.question: During an incident investigation, an IS auditor finds firewall, server and database logs disagree on event times by up to 40 minutes. Which control BEST addresses this?

options.A: Extend log retention on every system to two full years
options.B: Synchronize system clocks to an authoritative time source
options.C: Record each system's clock offset in the incident runbook
options.D: Send every system's logs to a central store for correlation

questions.key_concept: Log correlation and incident timelines need every system's clock synchronized to a common authoritative time source.
questions.pre_read: Notice the logs disagree on time. Ask which option fixes the timestamps rather than only collecting or keeping them.
questions.correct_explanation: Event timelines depend on every log using the same clock. Synchronizing all systems to a common authoritative time source makes timestamps comparable, so investigators can show what happened in what order and the logs hold up as evidence. Sending logs to a central store helps correlation, but it gathers the same mismatched timestamps, so events still cannot be reliably ordered.

wrong_explanations.A: Longer retention keeps more logs, but their timestamps would still disagree, so events still could not be ordered.
wrong_explanations.C: Recorded offsets drift and vary by system and date, so manual correction stays error-prone and the logs remain weak evidence.
wrong_explanations.D: Central collection, like clock sync, aims at one reliable timeline. Aggregation carries source quality forward, though; it cannot add accuracy the source lacked.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps logs longer without fixing their times, and C corrects times by hand from offsets that drift.
Final two: B beats D because synchronized clocks fix timestamps at the source, while a central store only gathers the mismatched times.
Exam cue: logs are evidence only if they can be trusted and put in order; fix integrity and timing at the source.

questions.question: Red team exercises keep evading detection, but defenders learn little because findings arrive months later in a written report. Which approach should the IS auditor recommend to address this BEST?

options.A: An annual vulnerability scan of internet-facing systems
options.B: A tabletop exercise on executive incident decisions
options.C: A purple team exercise pairing attackers with defenders
options.D: A longer red team engagement covering a broader scope

questions.key_concept: Purple teaming combines attack emulation with live defender feedback, so detection gaps are fixed during the exercise rather than months later.
questions.pre_read: Notice the problem is slow learning, not weak attacks. Ask which approach puts attackers and defenders in the same room.
questions.correct_explanation: The weakness is not the red team's skill but the feedback loop: defenders see results months later. A purple team exercise has attackers run techniques while defenders watch, tune detections and retest on the spot, turning each evasion into an improved control. A longer red team engagement would find more gaps, but the delayed written report would leave the learning problem unchanged.

wrong_explanations.A: Vulnerability scans find missing patches and misconfigurations. They do not exercise or improve detection of an active attacker.
wrong_explanations.B: Tabletops test decision-making, not whether technical detections catch real attack techniques.
wrong_explanations.D: More red team time finds more gaps, but results still arrive late in a report, so defenders keep learning slowly.

tips: Eliminate: A finds weaknesses but tests no detection, and B tests decisions rather than technical detection.
Final two: C beats D because the problem is slow feedback; more red teaming finds more gaps but still teaches late.
Exam cue: match the exercise to the stated weakness; when defenders are not learning, choose the collaborative format.

tips: Eliminate: A and D strengthen perimeter or host defenses without adding any visibility of internal traffic.

questions.question: A cloud service provider has contained a breach and confirmed which 47 business customers' personal data was exposed; those customers face their own regulatory deadlines. What should the IS auditor recommend management do FIRST?

options.A: Notify the affected customers now with the confirmed facts
options.B: Post a general breach notice on the public status page
options.C: Finish the forensic investigation before contacting any customer
options.D: File breach reports with each customer's regulator on their behalf

questions.key_concept: A provider that confirms a breach of customer data should notify the affected customers promptly so they can meet their own obligations.
questions.pre_read: Notice what is already confirmed and whose deadlines are running. Ask who needs to know first.
questions.correct_explanation: The 47 customers control the exposed data and face their own regulatory deadlines, which they cannot meet until they are told. Notifying them now with the confirmed facts, and updating them as forensics finishes, lets them act in time. Completing the investigation first is a cautious instinct, but the deciding facts are already confirmed, and waiting could make customers miss their deadlines.

wrong_explanations.B: A general notice does not give the 47 customers the specific facts they need to assess their own exposure and meet their deadlines.
wrong_explanations.C: Completing forensics first is usual when the affected parties are still unknown; once they are known, the clock that matters is theirs, not the investigation's.
wrong_explanations.D: The customers control the data and their regulatory duties. The provider supports them but should not file on their behalf.

tips: Eliminate: D takes over duties that belong to the customers, and B posts a general notice instead of telling the affected customers directly.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews how the forensic team images laptops seized in investigations. Which finding should concern the auditor MOST?

options.A: Analysts examine working copies rather than the master image
options.B: Imaging is performed by one analyst without a second witness
options.C: Commercial imaging tools are used instead of open-source tools
options.D: Original drives are connected without a write-blocker

questions.key_concept: A write-blocker keeps the original drive unchanged during imaging; without it, the evidence itself may be altered in ways no later step can undo.
questions.pre_read: Ask which weakness changes the original evidence itself, and which only weakens the paperwork around it.
questions.correct_explanation: Connecting an original drive without a write-blocker lets the operating system write to it, changing timestamps and other data on the evidence itself. That alteration cannot be undone and gives opposing counsel a strong integrity challenge. A missing second witness weakens chain-of-custody records, but the image can still be verified against the original by hash values, so it is the lesser risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Working on copies protects the master image and is recommended practice, so this finding is not a weakness.
wrong_explanations.B: A witness strengthens custody records, but integrity can still be shown by comparing hash values of the original and the image.
wrong_explanations.C: Tool choice is not a control weakness. Validated commercial and open-source imaging tools are both acceptable.

tips: Eliminate: A describes good practice, and C is a tool preference rather than a control weakness.
Final two: D beats B because writing to the original alters evidence permanently, while a missing witness is a documentation gap.
Exam cue: in evidence handling, a flaw that changes the original outranks a flaw in the paperwork around it.

questions.question: Investigators extracted an employee's company phone, but key messages had been synced to the employee's personal cloud account and deleted from the device. What would the IS auditor expect investigators to do FIRST?

options.A: Run a deeper physical extraction of the phone to recover the deletions
options.B: Involve legal counsel to preserve the cloud copy lawfully
options.C: Have IT export the cloud copy through the phone's synced session
options.D: Report that the deleted messages no longer exist as evidence

questions.key_concept: Phone evidence often lives in personal cloud sync accounts; preserve it promptly through counsel and lawful process, never by logging in.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the messages now live. Ask which lawful step secures them before the cloud copy can change.
questions.correct_explanation: The messages were deleted from the phone but still exist in the cloud account, where the employee or retention settings could remove them. Having counsel send preservation demands and, if needed, seek a court order secures that copy lawfully; private parties generally cannot compel a provider directly. A deeper physical extraction may recover fragments, but recovery is uncertain and does nothing to stop the cloud copy being lost.

wrong_explanations.A: Physical extraction is an accepted way to recover deletions, but the cloud still holds an intact copy: preserve the most complete evidence at risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Using the company phone's live session feels within the firm's rights, but it still enters a personal account without legal authority, risking inadmissible evidence.
wrong_explanations.D: The messages still exist in the cloud account, so declaring them lost abandons evidence that can be preserved.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because C reaches a personal account without legal authority, and D declares lost evidence that still exists in the cloud.
Final two: B beats A because the cloud copy is the reliable source; device recovery is uncertain and leaves it at risk.
Exam cue: evidence in a personal account is preserved through counsel before it can be deleted; never sign in to it yourself.

questions.question: Customer data in a bank's public cloud was stolen through a firewall rule the bank's own team had misconfigured. Which conclusion is MOST appropriate for the IS auditor?

options.A: The provider is accountable because the breach happened on its platform
options.B: The bank is accountable because it owns its own configuration
options.C: Accountability is shared because the provider's platform was used
options.D: The breach is outside audit scope because the data was outsourced

questions.key_concept: In the shared responsibility model, customers own the security of what they configure in the cloud and remain accountable for their data.
questions.pre_read: Notice who misconfigured the rule. Ask which layer of the cloud stack that setting belongs to.
questions.correct_explanation: Under the shared responsibility model, the provider secures the underlying cloud infrastructure, while the customer secures what it configures in the cloud, including firewall rules. The bank's own team set the faulty rule, so the bank is accountable. Shared accountability sounds balanced because the provider's platform was involved, but responsibility is divided by layer, and this failure sits wholly in the customer's layer.

wrong_explanations.A: The provider secures its infrastructure, not the customer's settings. A breach on the platform is not automatically the provider's failure.
wrong_explanations.C: The provider does share responsibility for the infrastructure layer, yet the bank configured this rule, and whoever configures a control answers for it.
wrong_explanations.D: Outsourcing hosting does not outsource accountability for data. Cloud-hosted data stays within the bank's control environment and audit scope.

tips: Eliminate: A blames the provider for a customer setting, and D assumes outsourcing removes the data from audit scope.
Final two: B beats C because shared responsibility divides duties by layer, and this rule sits in the bank's layer.
Exam cue: in cloud questions, ask who configured the failing control; that party is responsible for it, and the customer stays accountable for its data either way.
